items.passage: Last Tuesday, Mina left her umbrella on the bus. It was a blue umbrella with a wooden handle, and it had been a birthday present from her sister. At first she thought it was gone forever. The next morning, however, the bus company called. A driver had found the umbrella and kept it in the office. Mina walked to the station after work and collected it. She was so happy that she brought the driver a box of tea.
items.question: What did Mina lose?
items.evidence: Mina left her umbrella on the bus.

items.passage: Every Saturday morning, a community centre in Leeds opens its doors to broken things. At the Repair Cafe, volunteers with practical skills try to fix lamps, radios, chairs and clothes that visitors bring in. The service is free, but visitors are encouraged to stay and watch. "We want people to learn how things work," says the organiser. Since the cafe opened two years ago, it has repaired more than six hundred objects. Not everything can be saved, and some repairs take several visits. Still, the volunteers say the most valuable result is the conversations that happen around the tables.
items.question: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Volunteers fix things and teach visitors.
items.evidence: volunteers with practical skills try to fix ... visitors are encouraged to stay and watch.

items.passage: On-demand delivery services promise to save time, but the convenience is rarely free. Behind each quick delivery stands a network of couriers whose schedules are shaped by algorithms rather than fixed shifts. Economists debate whether such work offers genuine flexibility or simply shifts risk onto the workers. What is clear is that the price shown to customers covers only part of the arrangement. When a delivery is late, the courier may bear the cost; when demand falls, hours disappear. Regulators are now asking who should be responsible for the gaps that the app does not show.
items.question: What is the main point of the passage?
options: Delivery apps have made work less flexible.
Convenience involves costs that customers do not fully see.
items.evidence: the price shown to customers covers only part of the arrangement.

items.passage: Urban trees are often discussed as decoration, yet their value is increasingly measured in degrees and dollars. A mature tree can lower street temperatures, absorb storm water and improve air quality; in dense neighbourhoods, the difference can be a matter of health rather than comfort. The benefits are also unevenly distributed. Wealthier districts tend to have older, larger trees, while poorer areas often have fewer and younger ones. Planting programmes that ignore this pattern may widen the gap they claim to close. The difficult question is therefore not whether trees help, but who gets to benefit from them.
items.question: What is the main argument?
options: Tree planting must consider who benefits.
Cities should cut down old trees.
Air quality is unrelated to trees.
items.evidence: The difficult question is therefore not whether trees help, but who gets to benefit from them.
